set.hook: Lefteris Lazarou's seafood room on the Mikrolimano quay, the top-scored Greek-cuisine kitchen of 2026.
set.why: Lefteris Lazarou, a ship's cook's son who first cooked at sea at fifteen, opened Varoulko in 1987 and in 2002 won the first MICHELIN Star ever given to Greek cooking. The Star was gone by the Athens 2024 selection, which lists the room without one. Greek critics did not follow: in May 2026 Athinorama's Greek Cuisine Awards again scored it 16/20, the highest Greek-cuisine mark in the country. The seaside room on the Mikrolimano boardwalk opened in 2013.
set.hours: Call ahead: the MICHELIN listing gives daily 13:00-24:00; Mes Prestiges (checked May 2026) gives Tue-Sun 13:00-24:00, closed Monday; other undated listings give daily 12:30-24:00 or 13:00-01:00

set.hook: A third-generation Mikrolimano fish house from 1932, built on raw shellfish and fish salt-grilled over coals.
set.why: Giorgos Dourabeis, from Ios, and Rallia, from Kythira, opened this fish house on the harbour in 1932; their grandsons Sergios, Kostas and Rallis run it now. A 2005 renovation stripped out the old taverna look, which is why the room reads formal rather than rustic. The FNL Guide kept it among its starred Athens tables in 2026, and in 2023 the Brazilian chef Alex Atala of D.O.M. in Sao Paulo chose it for an Athens meal and posted about it.

set.hook: Chef Giorgos Papaioannou's Mikrolimano waterfront room, where the day's catch is grilled and left alone.
set.why: Giorgos Papaioannou learned to cook fish from his father in an early-1990s back-street shop near the port, then moved the flagship onto the Mikrolimano waterfront in spring 2013. He still buys the catch at the market himself. The name has since spread to Kefalari, Kavouri and a Mykonos outpost under the Okyalos group, and in May 2026 Athinorama's Greek Cuisine Awards scored the Mikrolimano room 14.5 out of 20.

set.hook: A 1944 fried-fish room by the Naval Academy with no menu, no bookings and the family's own retsina.
set.why: Margaro, a woman from Ano Mera on Mykonos, started frying fish on this corner in 1944. Her son Lazaros took over in 1974 and cut the list to what it still is: four or five fried catches, a Greek salad and retsina from the family's vines in Markopoulo. Her grandchildren work the pans now. Guides list shrimp, crayfish, red mullet, koutsomoura and lithrini, all pan-fried and never grilled, with tables spilling into the street in good weather.

set.hook: A Kastella hilltop fish taverna since 1957, looking down over the port and out to the Saronic.
set.why: Before it was a taverna it was a 1930s kafenio selling coffee and snacks to the Kastella neighbourhood. In 1957 Paraschos Manioudakis, a Cretan who had come to Piraeus for dock work, turned it into a taverna beside the chapel of Profitis Ilias. His grandson later renovated the room and kept the menu as it was. The terrace appears in the 1971 heist film The Burglars, and on a clear day the view runs from the Acropolis to Aegina.

set.hook: A canteen inside the Keratsini fish auction, frying and grilling the morning's catch beside the docks.
set.why: The Keratsini ichthyoskala has stood on the Iraklis harbour since 1965 and auctions fish every day of the year. Vasilis and Valbona, who came from Albania as newlyweds, took over its abandoned canteen in 2018 and rebuilt it from tarps and pallets; their daughter Alexandra works the tables. He crosses to the opposite dock around 3 a.m. to choose the fish, and octopus charred over coals is what the regulars order.

set.hook: A husband-and-wife ouzeri on Keratsini's little harbour, cooking what the local caiques landed.
set.why: Chrysa and Giorgos have kept this ouzeri on Keratsini's little harbour for more than thirty years, under the chimney of the closed DEH power station and in sight of the COSCO container cranes. The supply line is short: the harbour's fishermen eat half of what they land and sell Giorgos the rest, so the red mullet and anchovies are usually that morning's. Ask what is best today and they will tell you plainly.

set.hook: A former ship captain's small seafood ouzeri in Hatzikyriakio, its walls hung with his maritime collection.
set.why: Andreas Kontsos captained ships out of Kimolos before he cooked, and he kept what the sea left him: anchors, ropes, ocean-liner memorabilia. After running the 1990s Piraeus spot Karpouzi, he opened this small room in a former nautical warehouse and named it after the liners that carried Greek emigrants to Australia. On good nights there is ladenia, the Kimolos tomato-and-onion flatbread, next to the charcoal sardines.

set.hook: A producer-led meze room in a 1920 Freattyda neoclassical, with a roof terrace in summer.
set.why: The house is a 1920 neoclassical built by an architect who arrived by boat from Constantinople and settled in Freattyda. Since September 2015 it has been a meze room run by Stelios Parashos, with Nikos Omaris, trained at Selini on Santorini, building the menu from small named producers: staka from Crete, fava from Schinousa, kasseri from Xanthi, cured ham from Evrytania. In summer the tables move up to a roof terrace.

set.hook: An Ikarian sailors' kafenio near the port gates: tsipouro, tavli and mezedes that arrive unasked.
set.why: For about seventy years this kafenio has poured for the Ikarian community of Piraeus, its walls covered with photographs and murals of the island. Sailors and shipyard hands come for tsipouro with cheese and olives brought from Ikaria. When the 1956 building on Akti Poseidonos that housed it was taken back for redevelopment, the regulars moved the whole kafenio a few streets inland; LiFO reported the move in August 2023. Nikos, 'the Ikarian', keeps the counter.

set.hook: A 1920 grocery and wine shop near the port, still pouring the family's own retsina beside simple fry-ups.
set.why: Aristeidis Papakonstantinou came down from Gardiki, near Trikala, and opened this grocery and wine shop in 1920; the same family has run it since. Holes in the metal shutter were left by German bullets during the Occupation and kept on purpose. The retsina is the family's own, and the plates are what a corner grocer would cook: fried liver, meatballs, potatoes under eggs. On some nights groups arrive with instruments and the room sings.
set.reservation: Walk in most days; book on live-music nights

set.hook: An 1896 stone wine-house in the Agios Dionysios back streets, with barrel wine and rebetiko history.
set.why: The stone walls, iron shutters and cellar barrels go back to 1896, when the house opened as an oinomageireio in the Agios Dionysios back streets; between the wars new owners ran it as a grocery-taverna known as Trichas's. LiFO counts it among ten Piraeus shops that wrote history and records that a song by the rebetis Michalis Genitsaris was first sung here. The barrels still hold the house wine, poured by the karafa.

set.hook: A 1958 koutouki in Palaia Kokkinia, its covered courtyard built around an old whitewashed fig tree.
set.why: The koutouki has cooked since 1958 in a lane above Thivon Street in Palaia Kokkinia, the quarter built by refugees after 1922. Its covered courtyard grows around a tall fig tree with a whitewashed trunk, among old tiles and small objects gathered over decades. The business registry names Eirini Vergopoulou as holder; the sign still carries the name of the original Antonis. Wine comes from the barrel by the karafa.
